title: Twelve Folds and the Exponential Wall
description: Why paper runs out so fast, the student who worked out exactly how fast, and the arithmetic of doubling

concepts.title: The Rule a Student Broke
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades, puzzle books and classroom lore repeated a confident rule: no sheet of paper, however large, can be folded in half more than seven or eight times. Britney Gallivan, a high school junior from Pomona, California, took up an extra-credit challenge to fold anything in half twelve times. In December 2001 she worked out the mathematics of why each fold is harder than the last. She succeeded first with a thin sheet of gold foil, and when her teacher pressed her to do it with paper, she used her analysis to plan the attempt.

In January 2002 she did it. She folded a single strip of toilet paper about 4,000 feet (1.2 km) long in half twelve times, always in the same direction, leaving a stack of 2 to the 12th power, or 4,096, layers. Her account, How to Fold Paper in Half Twelve Times, was published as a booklet by the Historical Society of Pomona Valley. About a decade later, students from St. Mark's School in Massachusetts reported 13 folds of a far longer strip in an attempt at MIT.

The old rule held for ordinary sheets, but it was stated as if it were a law of nature. Take office paper about 0.1 mm thick and 297 mm long and fold it in the same direction seven times. You now have 128 layers: a wad about 12.8 mm thick and only about 2.3 mm long, more than five times thicker than it is long, and the eighth fold has to bend that block. Gallivan asked how much paper twelve folds require.

concepts.title: Gallivan's Formula in Words
concepts.contentHtml:
A real fold is not a perfect line. When a stack bends through 180 degrees, every layer wraps around a half circle, and each outer layer must travel farther than the one inside it because it curves around everything beneath. Paper spent on those curves cannot take part in the next fold. Gallivan added up this consumption, fold after fold, into what she called a loss function.

For a long strip folded always in the same direction, her result gives the minimum length L for n folds of paper of thickness t. In words: L equals pi times t, divided by 6, times the quantity (2 to the n, plus 4), times the quantity (2 to the n, minus 1). Plug in small values and the multiplier of pi times t runs 1, 4, 14, 50, 186 and 714 for one to six folds. For twelve folds it is 2,798,250, so the strip must be roughly 8.8 million times longer than it is thick. For paper 0.1 mm thick that comes to almost 900 m, and Gallivan's 1.2 km roll left a margin.

The growth rate matters more than the constant. For large n, the product (2 to the n, plus 4) times (2 to the n, minus 1) behaves like 4 to the n, so each extra fold needs about four times as much paper as the one before; a 13th fold at the same thickness needs about 3.5 km. Gallivan also derived a separate formula for folding in alternating directions, where the width is halved only on every second fold. Both formulas rest on stated assumptions: layers of uniform thickness, half-circle bends and no stretching.

concepts.title: Doubling Outruns Intuition
concepts.contentHtml:
The thickness side of the story is the classic exponential. After n folds a stack has 2 to the n layers: ten folds give 1,024 and twenty give 1,048,576. Imagine, against all of Gallivan's arithmetic, that a sheet 0.1 mm thick could be folded 42 times. The stack would be about 440,000 km tall, beyond the Moon, whose average distance from Earth is about 384,400 km. At 51 folds it would pass the Sun, about 150 million km away. Each fold adds as much thickness as the whole stack already had.

Those numbers are thought experiments, and they hide the real obstacle. In single-direction folding the folded length halves each time while the thickness doubles, so the ratio of thickness to length grows by a factor of 4 per fold. That is the same factor of 4 that drives Gallivan's paper budget. Real material adds further limits, since fibers crack at tight bends and a thick stack stops behaving like a crease and starts behaving like a rolled bundle.

It helps to ask which quantity grows and by what factor. Thinner material shrinks the constant in front of the formula but not the factor of 4, which is why very thin gold foil made a sensible first target and why no material allows folding forever. Engineers who pack solar arrays or membrane telescopes into rockets face the same budget, because every fold spends material at the bend and thickness accumulates. Most origami mathematics assumes paper of zero thickness, and the later lessons point out where that assumption matters.

title: Folding Beats Ruler and Compass
description: Two problems the Greeks could not solve, the 1837 proof that closed them, and the folds that solve them anyway

concepts.title: Three Problems and an 1837 Verdict
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek geometers left three construction problems open: trisect any given angle, double the cube (build a cube with twice the volume of a given one, which means constructing the cube root of 2), and square the circle. A story told by ancient writers says the cube problem began when an oracle told the people of Delos to double an altar to end a plague; it is a legend, not history. Greek mathematicians did find solutions, but only by allowing extra tools, such as a marked ruler slid into position (neusis) or curves like the conic sections.

With an unmarked straightedge and a compass alone, the problems are impossible, and the proof came only in 1837 from the French mathematician Pierre Wantzel. Every straightedge-and-compass step intersects lines and circles, which amounts to solving an equation of degree at most 2. Constructible lengths are therefore built from whole numbers by adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing and taking square roots. The cube root of 2, and the cosine of 20 degrees needed to trisect a 60-degree angle, are roots of cubic equations that no chain of square roots can reach. Squaring the circle fell in 1882, when Ferdinand von Lindemann proved that pi is transcendental.

Paper folding escapes the verdict because a single fold can satisfy two alignments at once. In 1936 the Italian mathematician Margherita Beloch showed that the fold placing two given points onto two given lines can solve general cubic equations. Earlier, T. Sundara Row's Geometric Exercises in Paper Folding (1893) had shown how much of Euclid can be done by folding, though its trisection was only approximate.

concepts.title: Abe's Trisection and Messer's Cube Root
concepts.contentHtml:
The best-known folded trisection is credited to Hisashi Abe and was reported in Japan in 1980. Put the angle in the bottom-left corner of a square, between the bottom edge and a crease from the corner. Fold any horizontal crease and call its left end E. Fold the bottom edge up to that crease, unfold, and call the left end of the new middle crease G. Then fold the corner up so that E lands on the angle's crease and, at the same moment, the corner itself lands on the middle crease. You slide the paper until both alignments hold, just as a Greek neusis slides a marked ruler.

Unfold and draw lines from the corner to the spots where the corner and G landed. The first line makes one third of the angle with the bottom edge, the second two thirds. The reason is that the fold creates three congruent right triangles fanning out from the corner, each with a short side equal to the gap between the two horizontal creases. As described, the method works for acute angles; an obtuse angle can be handled by splitting off a right angle, because a third of a right angle, 30 degrees, is easy to fold.

Peter Messer published a folded cube root of 2 in 1986, as a problem in the journal Crux Mathematicorum. Crease a square into horizontal thirds. Then fold the bottom-right corner onto the left edge while the point where the lower crease meets the right edge lands on the upper crease. The corner's landing point divides the left edge so that the upper piece is the cube root of 2, about 1.26, times the lower piece.

concepts.title: Seven Ways to Make One Fold
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1989, at the First International Meeting of Origami Science and Technology in Ferrara, Italy, Humiaki Huzita described six basic ways to define a single fold by lining up points and lines: fold through two points; fold one point onto another; fold one line onto another; fold perpendicular to a line through a point; fold one point onto a line, through a second point; and fold two points onto two lines at once. Jacques Justin's paper in the same volume, in French, listed seven, but was widely overlooked. Koshiro Hatori publicized the seventh in the early 2000s: fold a point onto one line with the crease perpendicular to another line. Robert Lang later proved that the seven exhaust every way of defining one fold by such alignments.

The sixth operation, the Beloch fold, does the heavy lifting. With all seven, single folds can solve any polynomial equation up to degree 4, but not general equations of higher degree. That settles regular polygons too: a regular polygon with n sides can be folded exactly if and only if n is a power of 2 times a power of 3 times a product of distinct Pierpont primes, which are primes equal to a power of 2 times a power of 3, plus 1. So the heptagon (7 is 2 times 3, plus 1) and the nonagon fold, though neither can be drawn with straightedge and compass, while the 11-gon is out of reach.

Origami lengths are still algebraic numbers, so squaring the circle stays impossible. Moves that form two creases at once reach further: Lang used them to divide any angle into five equal parts, and in 2009 Roger Alperin and Lang extended the theory to such multi-fold moves.

title: When Does It Fold Flat?
description: Two rules any folder can check with a pencil, and why the global question is computationally hard

concepts.title: Count the Mountains: Maekawa's Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Fold a square napkin in half, then in half again, and unfold it. Four creases now radiate from the center. Seen from one side, three of them are valleys, which sink away from you, and one is a mountain, which rises toward you. A waterbomb base has six creases at its center when unfolded: the four halves of the diagonals are one type and the two halves of one midline are the other. The difference is two both times.

Maekawa's theorem says that at every interior vertex of a crease pattern that folds flat, the numbers of mountain creases M and valley creases V differ by exactly two: M minus V equals 2 or minus 2. One proof looks at a tiny circle drawn around the vertex. Folded flat, the circle squashes into a flat polygon with one corner per crease, and each corner measures either 0 or 360 degrees, depending on the crease type. The angles of a polygon with M plus V corners must add up to (M plus V, minus 2) times 180 degrees, which forces M minus V to be plus or minus 2.

Every interior vertex of a flat-foldable pattern has an even number of creases, so a vertex where five creases meet can never fold flat. And the regions of any flat-foldable pattern can be colored with two colors so that neighbors always differ, matching the faces that end up facing up or down. The theorem carries Jun Maekawa's name, but S. Murata published it in 1966 and Jacques Justin found it independently in 1986; the name spread through a 1987 book by Kunihiko Kasahara and Toshie Takahama.

concepts.title: Measure the Angles: Kawasaki's Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Counting creases is not enough; the angles between them matter too. Kawasaki's theorem handles a single vertex in the middle of a flat sheet with an even number of creases, numbered in order around the point. Such a vertex can be folded flat, with some choice of mountains and valleys, if and only if the alternating sum of the angles between consecutive creases is zero: the first angle minus the second plus the third, and so on around. Since all the angles add up to 360 degrees, this is the same as saying that every other angle adds up to exactly 180 degrees.

Try it with four creases. Angles of 45, 90, 135 and 90 degrees, in that order, pass: 45 plus 135 is 180, and 90 plus 90 is 180. Angles of 100, 80, 70 and 110 degrees fail, because the alternate angles sum to 170 and 190. The reason is easy to picture. Let an ant walk once around the vertex on the folded paper. Each crease reverses its direction, so it sweeps the first angle one way, the second angle back, and so on. To end where it started, the forward and backward sweeps must cancel.

A companion rule, the big-little-big lemma, constrains the mountains and valleys: if one angle is strictly smaller than both of its neighbors, the two creases bounding it must be of opposite types. Like Maekawa's, the theorem's name simplifies its history. Murata had the four- and six-crease cases in 1966; S. A. Robertson, Jacques Justin and Toshikazu Kawasaki found the general case independently between the late 1970s and 1989; and Kawasaki himself has credited Kôdi Husimi, who studied the four-crease case.

concepts.title: Local Rules, Global Trouble
concepts.contentHtml:
Maekawa's and Kawasaki's conditions are local: each checks one vertex at a time and can be tested with a protractor. A full crease pattern can pass both tests at every vertex and still refuse to fold flat, because the layers must also stack in some order without paper passing through paper. In 1994 Thomas Hull conjectured that the local checks plus one simple test on an associated graph would settle the global question. Marshall Bern and Barry Hayes showed otherwise in 1996, in a paper titled "The Complexity of Flat Origami."

They proved that deciding whether a general crease pattern can be folded flat is NP-hard, both when mountains and valleys are left open and when they are specified in advance. NP-hard means that a fast general method for this problem would also give fast methods for thousands of notoriously difficult problems, from scheduling to logic puzzles; no such method is known, and most computer scientists believe none exists. The difficulty sits in the layer order: a choice made at one end of the sheet can force or forbid choices far away.

The story has a coda. In 2016 a team including Hugo Akitaya, Erik Demaine, Thomas Hull and Tomohiro Tachi reported an error in one of the 1996 gadgets and gave corrected proofs, showing that the problem stays NP-hard even for box pleating, where creases lie on a square grid and its diagonals. Some special cases are easy, though. For a rectangular map creased along a grid, with every crease's direction assigned, a computer can decide in linear time whether it folds flat by a sequence of simple folds.

title: One Straight Cut
description: From a 1721 Japanese puzzle book and a flag legend to a theorem that cuts any straight-sided shape with one snip

concepts.title: A Star, a Flag and a Legend
concepts.contentHtml:
American schoolchildren are often told that Betsy Ross, a Philadelphia upholsterer, showed George Washington how to make a five-pointed star with a single snip of the scissors, persuading him to drop six-pointed stars from the first national flag. The story first appeared in public in 1870, when her grandson William Canby presented a paper to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania based on family memories, close to a century after the events. An 1873 article in Harper's New Monthly Magazine spread the folding detail. No document from the 1770s supports the visit, and historians treat the tale as family legend. What the records do show is a May 1777 payment to Elizabeth Ross for making ships' colors for the Pennsylvania navy.

The trick itself is real and older than the legend. The earliest known fold-and-cut problem appears in Wakoku Chiyekurabe (Mathematical Contests), a Japanese puzzle book published in 1721 by Kan Chu Sen, which asks for a family crest to be cut from a folded sheet with one straight cut. Harry Houdini's Paper Magic (1922) included a five-pointed star; the origami historian David Lister suggested that the book was ghostwritten, possibly by Walter Gibson. Gerald Loe's Paper Capers (1955), a book of paper magic, went further, cutting whole arrangements of shapes, such as a ring of stars.

Martin Gardner brought the problem to mathematicians in his Scientific American column in 1960. He reported that Loe could cut out any letter of the alphabet and asked the general question: which shapes can be produced by folding a sheet flat and making one complete straight cut?

concepts.title: The Fold-and-Cut Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The answer is all of them, as long as the sides are straight. The fold-and-cut theorem says that any finite pattern of straight line segments drawn on a sheet of paper can be cut out by folding the sheet flat and making a single complete straight cut. The pattern may be one polygon, convex or not, several separate polygons, polygons with holes, polygons sharing edges, or even stray segments. The folding must do something precise: it must bring every drawn segment onto one common line, and bring no other paper onto that line, so that the cut slices exactly the drawing and nothing more.

Two proofs appeared in the late 1990s. Erik Demaine, his father Martin Demaine and Anna Lubiw used the straight skeleton. Imagine every edge of the shape moving inward at the same speed while staying parallel to itself, like a lake shrinking evenly from its shore. The corners trace out a branching network of lines, the skeleton. Those lines, plus creases running perpendicular to the edges, form a crease pattern that folds flat and lines up all the edges. A second method, by Marshall Bern, Erik Demaine, David Eppstein and Barry Hayes, packs disks onto the paper so that lines joining the centers of touching disks divide the sheet into triangles and quadrilaterals, then folds each piece with a standard crease unit called a molecule.

The theorem lives in the idealized world of origami mathematics, where paper has zero thickness and can take any number of layers. The folding it prescribes for a complicated letter may be hopeless by hand. What it guarantees is that a folding exists, and an algorithm finds the folds.

concepts.title: Cutting a Square, Step by Step
concepts.contentHtml:
A square drawn in the middle of a sheet shows the idea in its simplest form, using symmetry. Fold the sheet in half along the horizontal line through the square's center, so the square's top and bottom edges lie on top of each other. Fold in half again along the vertical center line, so its left and right edges coincide too. What remains visible of the square's outline is an L-shaped pair of half-edges meeting at a corner. Fold along the 45-degree line from the center through that corner, and the two half-edges land on one another. Now all four sides lie along a single short segment, and no other paper touches the line through it. One straight cut along that line removes the square.

Most shapes lack such symmetry, which is where the general theory earns its keep. For a triangle, the creases are the three angle bisectors, which meet at the center of the inscribed circle and continue out past the corners, plus a crease from that center perpendicular to each side, also running out to the edge of the paper. For a shape like the letter R, the skeleton branches many times and the perpendicular creases bend at every skeleton line they cross, which is why practical patterns are computed rather than found by hand.

Symmetry also explains the five-pointed star of the Betsy Ross story. A regular star has five mirror lines through its center. Folding along them packs the sheet into a narrow wedge, one tenth of the full turn, in which all ten edges of the star lie on a single segment, ready for one angled cut.

title: Designing by Mathematics
description: How origami gained a written language, then a geometry of trees and circles that computers can work with

concepts.title: Yoshizawa and the Language of Diagrams
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the oldest known books of folding instructions, Hiden Senbazuru Orikata (1797), presents 49 designs of connected cranes, credited to a Buddhist priest, Gido, of Ise Province. Its pictures are hard to follow. The modern craft owes its written language largely to Akira Yoshizawa (1911 to 2005), who left factory work in 1937 to devote himself to folding and spent about two decades in poverty, selling preserved food door to door, before a 1952 commission for the magazine Asahi Graph made his name.

His 1954 monograph Atarashii Origami Geijutsu (New Origami Art) set out a system of lines and arrows. Samuel Randlett and Robert Harbin adopted and extended it, and Randlett's The Art of Origami (1961) carried it to English readers. Now the international standard, it is called the Yoshizawa-Randlett system. A valley fold is a dashed line, and a mountain fold is a dash-dot line, with one or two dots per dash depending on the author. Yoshizawa also developed wet-folding, dampening thick paper so that it holds rounded, sculpted forms. In 1989 he estimated that he had made more than 50,000 models; only a few hundred were published as diagrams in his books.

A diagram records a sequence of moves. Mathematicians and modern designers often prefer a different record, the crease pattern: the unfolded sheet showing every crease of the finished model or base at once. Jun Maekawa did much to popularize crease patterns as a design tool, and they are exactly the objects that the flat-folding theorems describe.

concepts.title: Trees, Circles and Flaps
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Lang, a physicist who joined NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1988 and holds 46 patents in lasers and optics, left engineering in 2001 to fold full time. His central tool is tree theory. Draw the subject as a stick figure, such as a beetle's body with six legs and two antennae; each stick end is a flap. The goal is a uniaxial base, a folded shape whose flaps all lie along one axis and whose outline matches the stick figure.

Each flap tip comes from a point on the square, and folding never stretches paper. So for any two tips, their distance apart on the unfolded square must be at least the length of the path between them along the stick figure. For flaps meeting at one body point, this means that a flap of length L claims a circle of radius L around its tip's point, and those circles cannot overlap. Circles may hang off the edge of the sheet: only their centers must lie on it. A corner flap uses a quarter circle of paper, an edge flap a half circle and a middle flap a full one, which is why long flaps tend to go at corners. Longer internal sticks become rivers, bands of paper between groups of circles, a technique that Lang and Toshiyuki Meguro developed in the 1990s.

Lang's program TreeMaker, begun around 1990, turns this into an optimization: place the points to make the flaps as long as possible, then compute the creases. A small check: four quarter circles of radius one half at the corners of a unit square touch at the midpoints of the edges, allowing four corner flaps each half a side long.

concepts.title: What Computers Can and Cannot Do
concepts.contentHtml:
Before such tools, complexity came from intuition and persistence. Lang's Black Forest Cuckoo Clock, composed in 1987 in Ludwigsburg, Germany, folds from one uncut rectangle ten times as long as it is wide and stood for years among the most complex origami figures ever made. His book Origami Design Secrets (2003) later set out the tree methods so that other folders could design at that level deliberately.

Mathematics also marks the limits of automation. In 2010 Erik Demaine, Sándor Fekete and Lang proved that deciding whether a given set of circles can be packed into a square is NP-hard, so the optimization at the heart of TreeMaker has no known fast exact method. Programs search for good packings instead. Many designers now work on a square grid with 45-degree diagonals, a style called box pleating, in which flaps and creases snap to regular positions and are easier to plan and to fold.

At the other extreme, existence is guaranteed. A result presented in 1999 showed that every polyhedral shape can be folded from a large enough square of paper, though the method wastes most of the sheet. Tomohiro Tachi's Origamizer software, released in 2008, produced practical folds of complex surfaces such as the Stanford bunny, a standard test model in computer graphics. In 2017 Demaine and Tachi proved that the approach can fold any oriented polyhedral surface watertight, without gaps, while folding each convex face seamlessly from one piece of the sheet.

title: Folding Goes to Work
description: Folds that open satellites, stents that open in the body, and origami with no paper at all

concepts.title: The Map That Opens in One Pull
concepts.contentHtml:
A sheet creased in the Miura pattern opens fully when you pull two opposite ends apart and closes again when you push them together. The pattern is a grid of congruent parallelograms: along one direction the creases run straight, along the other they zigzag, and every zigzag line is entirely mountains or entirely valleys while the straight lines alternate. It is named for Koryo Miura (born 1930), an astrophysicist at the University of Tokyo and Japan's Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, who developed it with Masamori Sakamaki in the 1970s for packing large membranes in space. A 1980 article by Ian Bain in New Scientist described the Miura-ori map.

The Miura fold is rigid origami: it can open through a continuous motion in which every parallelogram stays perfectly flat and only the creases act as hinges, so stiff panels such as solar cells can be used. Its folding motion has a single degree of freedom, so one pull or one motor can deploy the whole sheet. In 2013 Mark Schenk and Simon Guest showed that Miura-folded sheets have a negative Poisson's ratio in the plane: stretched in one direction, they expand in the other instead of narrowing.

On March 18, 1995, an H-II rocket launched Japan's Space Flyer Unit from Tanegashima. Among its experiments was a two-dimensional deployable solar array folded in Miura's pattern. About ten months later, in January 1996, the astronaut Koichi Wakata used the robotic arm of the Space Shuttle Endeavour to capture the satellite and bring it home. It is now displayed at the National Museum of Nature and Science in Tokyo.

concepts.title: Stents, Airbags and Telescopes
concepts.contentHtml:
Folding helps wherever something large must pass through something small. In 2006 Kaori Kuribayashi, Zhong You and colleagues at Oxford and Toyohashi University of Technology described a self-deploying origami stent graft: a tube of nickel-titanium shape-memory foil, creased in a repeating fold pattern so that it could be packed narrow for insertion and then open itself to full size. You's group later tackled a gap in the mathematics, which assumes zero thickness. In a 2015 paper in Science, Yan Chen, Rui Peng and You showed how to hinge thick panels so that they reproduce exactly the motions of zero-thickness origami.

Airbags show a subtler use. Crash simulations must start from an airbag folded into its small packet, and to get there the software first has to flatten the bag's three-dimensional shape, a problem much like folding one flat shape into another. The German engineering firm EASi adopted Lang's universal molecule algorithm, taken from tree theory, to compute those flattened states. Here the origami mathematics serves the computer model of the airbag, not the physical folding.

The most ambitious proposal was Eyeglass, a space telescope studied at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory from around 2000. Its lens was to be a thin diffractive membrane 100 meters across, folded to fit a rocket payload space about 4 meters wide. Lang helped adapt an umbrella-like folding pattern, and the team built and tested a 5-meter prototype, but the project did not go beyond that stage.

concepts.title: Origami Without Creases: DNA
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2006 Paul Rothemund of Caltech published a method he called DNA origami in Nature. He took a long single strand of DNA, the genome of a virus called M13 that infects bacteria, about 7,000 bases long, and designed more than 200 short "staple" strands, each made to bind separate stretches of the long strand and pin them together. Mixed in solution, staples and scaffold assembled themselves in a single step into shapes about 100 nanometers across: squares, disks, five-pointed stars and smiley faces. Each staple could serve as a pixel about 6 nanometers wide, so the shapes could carry patterns such as words and images on their surfaces.

The name is partly a metaphor. Nothing is creased. The design step works like raster scanning: the scaffold is routed back and forth through the whole shape, like a single line filling in a picture, and the staples hold neighboring passes together. None of the flat-folding theorems apply. What survives from paper origami is the core idea of one long continuous piece, never cut, shaped entirely by which parts are brought together.

The method spread quickly. Nadrian Seeman had proposed DNA as a building material in the early 1980s. In 2009 Shawn Douglas, William Shih and colleagues extended the scaffold-and-staple approach to three-dimensional shapes. In 2012 Douglas, Ido Bachelet and George Church reported a hinged DNA nanorobot closed by aptamer locks that act as a logic gate: in tests on cells in culture, it opened to present its cargo of antibody fragments only when it sensed the right combination of molecules on a cell's surface.
